17.10.5.en: * ["My soul is in my hand"]... A man's soul is between his hands when he is in the midst of dangers... So the righteous man says: As for me, I die daily, I am in constant danger because of (my attachment to) Your word, and for the sake of the truth... But I have not forgotten Your law, for the danger of death cannot make me forget Your law.

17.10.6.en: We can understand this statement in another way, namely that my soul is always in my palm, that is, it is always practicing good works, for the "hand" or the "palm" always denotes work.

17.10.7.en: Origen * You gain the world of light instead of a bitter pain that you bear for His sake for one day.

17.10.8.en: If you endure hunger a little for love of Him, your desire to see His face will then be kindled.

17.10.9.en: If darkness appears on your face from works done for Him, He will adorn you with His glory forever without end.

17.10.10.en: If you strip yourself of what is yours, He will clothe you with His light, and hide from you what is yours.

17.10.11.en: If you leave what you possess, you will possess it in yourself eternally.

17.10.13.en: * The toil of all the long years of this present life disappears when we look to the eternity of the glory to come, and all our sorrows will vanish by thinking of the great blessing, and become like vapor that dissolves as though it had never been; like lightning that disappears as soon as it flashes.

17.10.14.en: St. John Cassian * They (the martyrs) renounced all the things that are on earth, and saw with the eyes of faith the King of heaven, and the ranks of angels standing before Him. They pictured in their minds heaven and its unutterable blessings. They transferred their thoughts to heaven, and gave no more attention to anything they could see with their bodily eyes...

17.10.15.en: They were never affected by the visible things (the instruments of torture), but passed beside them, counting them dreams and shadows, and their minds gained wings because of their desire for the things to come.

17.10.16.en: * We do not fear poverty or sickness or any affliction of this kind, for we know that we are on our way to a better life, which is invulnerable to death and destruction, and free from all injustice.

17.11.0.en: St. John Chrysostom "They change the night into day: the light is near to the darkness" [12].

17.11.1.en: They speak to him about the night, where his days had almost passed, as though it were day, but it is not a day cheerful with its light; rather its light is near to the darkness. While he was not expecting anything on earth, they focused their talk on prosperity in the world as the Lord's reward to the righteous, and so they prepare for him in their minds the world as a house of rest, but he sees death before his eyes, and has no hope in the temporal matters of the world. He welcomes death as a house in which to settle. There in the grave his bed is made ready.

17.12.0.en: "If I wait, the grave is mine house: I have made my bed in the darkness" [13].

17.13.0.en: "I have said to the grave, Thou art my father: to the worm, Thou art my mother, and my sister" [14].

17.13.1.en: In bitterness Job looks to exchange his friends in the world for the grave, which becomes a father to him, since it is more merciful than they, and in place of their promises of temporal blessings he finds in the worm his mother and his sister. Job complained that his relatives had failed him and become strangers to him (Job 19:13-14), therefore he mentions here relatives who do not leave him or disown him, namely death and the worm.

17.13.2.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem sees that Job called corruption a mother and a sister, because on account of sin the sentence was passed against man to dissolve and decay and return to his dust.

17.13.3.en: * If we understand this in the spiritual sense, nature is not unfittingly called our mother, and habit is called our sister, for we were born from the one and grew with the other. The same mother and sister are the worm, for because of corrupt nature and evil habit we are bound to a kind of worm, or stirring thoughts, that eat the mind. For the corrupt nature of the body and evil habit give birth to many cares in the heart of our weakness, and so rightly they were called a worm.

17.13.5.en: * May we rid ourselves of the filth of sin, so that the first beauty of virtue may appear. David the prophet says in the Psalm: ["O Lord, by Your beauty You gave strength to my beauty"] (Ps 30:7). Let us be purified so that the image of God may appear in us, and this is what God wants of us, that we be without defilement, without lack and without blemish.

17.13.6.en: Fr. Dorotheus * All the saints grieve with daily sighs over this weakness of their nature. And while they search out their wandering thoughts and the hidden things of their consciences and their deep retreats, they cry out in supplication: "And enter not into judgment with thy servant: for in thy sight shall no man living be justified" (Ps 143:2)....

17.13.7.en: See, then, how all the saints truly confess that all men, as they themselves also are, are sinners, and yet they never despair of their salvation, but seek complete cleansing by the grace and mercy of God...

17.13.8.en: There is no one, however holy, in this life without sin. The teaching of the Savior, who gave His disciples the pattern of perfect prayer..., also told us this, for He says: "And forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive those who trespass against us" (Mt 6:12).

17.13.9.en: Therefore, since He gave this as a true prayer practiced by saints, as we must believe without the least doubt, who can remain stubborn, impudent and puffed up with the pride of Satan, supposing that he is without sin.

17.13.10.en: Fr. Theonas * Just as the saint is the temple of God, so the sinner makes of himself a tomb.

17.13.11.en: St. Jerome "And where is now my hope?"

17.14.0.en: "As for my hope, who shall see it?" [15]

17.14.1.en: Job sees that all his former hopes go down with him into the grave, and he laments them. Truly, if in this life only we have hope, we are of all men most miserable (1 Cor 15:19). There is no one who can see our hopes that console us, for we look not at the things which are seen and temporal, but at the things which are not seen and eternal (2 Cor 4:18).

17.14.2.en: The hopes his friends offered him go down with him into the grave, to be buried with him and not return. They are mortal and offer what is perishable.

17.14.3.en: * ["What then is my hope?"] [15]. Or where is the hope of man in whom this way of weakness is fulfilled? "Where shall I see my good things?" when we depart from it.

17.14.4.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * ["Where is now my expectation?"] [15]. What can be the righteous man's expectation but God, who justifies the righteous, who by His own will descended to human punishment, and by His righteousness freed the captives of death? For they will not cease from the rest of the expectations that are full of hope. They know that this is coming, but they ask for the speed of the coming. Therefore he did not say, "Where is my expectation?" but added the word "now," showing that he wishes that what will one day come may be fulfilled without delay.

17.14.5.en: ["And who considers my patience?"] [15]... The Truth bears witness: ["For I tell you, that many prophets and kings have desired to see those things which ye see, and have not seen them"] (Lk 10:24). And so, "who considers my patience?" The breaths of ardent desire have become open... Let him say: "Who considers my patience?" For what the Ruler of the matter (God) counts a short time, the one who loves sees as a long time.

17.14.7.en: * We ought to lay up in heaven what we lose now on earth. The enemy can dig through our houses, but can he break the door of heaven?! He kills the guard here, but can he kill God, its keeper?!

17.14.8.en: * If an architect told you that your house is falling down immediately, would you not move quickly before you are occupied with lamenting over it?! Behold, the Founder of the world tells you that the destruction of the world is near, and do you not believe Him...?! Listen to the voice of His prophecy: "Heaven and earth shall pass away" (Mt 24:35)... Listen to His counsel!

17.15.0.en: St. Augustine "They shall go down to the bars of the pit, when our rest together is in the dust" [16].

17.15.1.en: * ["Or will they go down with me to hell, or shall we go down together to the dust?"] [16]. Why then do we put up buildings?

17.15.2.en: Why do we trouble ourselves with costly coverings for couches and various garments? Why do we "lay field to field" (Isa 5:8)? Why do we seek riches that do not go with us?

17.15.3.en: And why do we not believe the plan of the Judge, and obey Him, who says: ["Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal"] (Mt 6:19-20). For our angels guard our treasures, and above all the Lord of the angels.

17.15.4.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * ["Do you not think that at least there will be rest for me there?"]... Here is what it profits us to meditate in great fear as a guarantee for us of eternal rest, for even Job was terrified of it... "And if the righteous scarcely be saved, where shall the ungodly and the sinner appear?" (1 Pet 4:18). For the blessed Job knew that he would receive rest after the blows of affliction, but as he shakes our hearts with fear, he seemed to be in doubt regarding the reward of eternal rest by saying: ["Do you not think?"]

17.15.6.en: * Some see their houses in which they live as their kingdom, and although they know that death is certain, and that one day it will force them to leave them, in their hearts they feel that they will remain forever. They boast of the size of their houses, and the excellent materials of which they are made. They find pleasure in decorating their houses with bright colors, and in choosing the sturdiest and best furniture to fill the rooms. They imagine that by owning a house that will last long... they will find in it their peace, that is, whenever they are sure that its walls and roofs remain solid for many generations.

17.15.7.en: But we, on the contrary, know that we are merely guests living temporarily on earth. We realize that the houses we dwell in are like hotels on the road to eternity. We do not seek peace or security from the material walls around us or the roofs over our heads. Rather we wish to surround ourselves with the walls of divine grace. And we look up to heaven on high as our roof. As for the furniture in our life, it should be good works, which we do in the spirit of love.

17.15.9.en: I look forward to meeting You

17.15.10.en: * Whenever I remember the day of my departure, or the day of my meeting with You, my soul is crushed within me, groaning because of every weakness that comes upon me.

17.15.11.en: Behold, the wicked grow fat, for they think they will live here forever.

17.15.12.en: But as for me, the day of Your last coming is engraved on my heart, and never leaves my memory.

17.15.13.en: By what shall I be justified before You?

17.15.14.en: * In the midst of my sorrow over my weakness, my heart rejoices within me.

17.15.15.en: Yes, I long to return to my eternal home!

17.15.16.en: My eyes look to You; when shall I meet You face to face?

17.15.17.en: * My God, behold, around me are those who seek dry debate.

17.15.18.en: They spoil my repentance, and my longing for the meeting with You.

17.15.19.en: No, rather the enemy of good, a stranger to me and to all the human race, has no work but to rob me of the enjoyment of thinking of You, and of preparing for the fellowship of the eternal glories.

17.15.20.en: He is a stubborn adversary, who does not rest until he brings me down with him to his eternal dwelling.

17.15.21.en: In this I do not justify myself, for You know that I am a sinner.

17.15.22.en: I am wounded by sin, but I have found You a healing Physician!

17.15.23.en: I am a sinner, I have found You the Holy One, sanctifying my whole being!

17.15.24.en: I am a debtor, and You are my surety and guarantor.

17.15.25.en: Your blood tears up the bond written against me.

17.15.26.en: Your cross frees me from my captivity.

17.15.27.en: You alone spoil principalities and powers, by Your cross You make a show of them openly, so I escape from their hands, and bow no more to their authority.

17.15.28.en: I depart from the ruler of this age, to take refuge under Your wings, O King of kings and Lord of lords.

17.15.29.en: The enemy of good thought that by wisdom he had captured and humbled me.

17.15.30.en: But his wisdom became malice and craftiness!

17.15.31.en: My Lord has taken from him true wisdom, since he cut himself off from the wisdom of God.

17.15.32.en: The wicked one became foolish, and lost his abilities.

17.15.33.en: But as for me, in my ignorance I cry out for help.

17.15.34.en: I long for union with You, O Wisdom of God.

17.15.35.en: I possess You, and so through You I become truly wise, and am made worthy to dwell in heaven, the dwelling of the wise!

17.15.36.en: * What grieves my soul is that the enemy of good captures many.

17.15.37.en: Every soul that loses Your light, I count myself in darkness with it!

17.15.38.en: And every soul that makes light of its salvation, I count myself as one who perishes with it!

17.15.39.en: Every soul that the enemy takes captive, I count myself a captive with it!

17.15.40.en: * Why does my soul groan when I see the wicked, who oppose the truth, prospering?

17.15.41.en: However long the time of their life, they will pass quickly, and like the grass they wither!

17.15.42.en: Your children are like a tree in the season of winter, appearing as dead trees without leaves or fruit, but the spring of Your day will come, and the frost of the world will go, and Your trees will be glorified with their wonderful fruit!

17.15.43.en: Truly. The world will soon pass away, and the eternal glory of Your children will appear!

17.15.44.en: However severe the frost of the world, and however the trials pile up, the earnest of heaven fills me with Your joy!

17.15.45.en: And fellowship with You even in Your sufferings fills me with peace!

17.15.47.en: Grant me to possess divine wisdom and truth.

17.15.48.en: That I may renounce arrogant human wisdom.

17.15.49.en: I enjoy You, O All-humble One!

17.15.50.en: * My soul is in my hands, and I walk in the midst of dangers.

17.15.51.en: I look forward with joy to my departure from the world at any moment!

17.15.52.en: I do not cease to accomplish Your work with my hands, for I am Your ambassador.

17.15.53.en: Until, when I depart, I am found with You, and enjoy Your splendor!

17.15.54.en: * Finally, let all my hope be in You.

17.15.55.en: Let my treasure be in Your heavens!

17.15.56.en: There is no place as safe as they!

18.0.0.en: 1 Then answered Bildad the Shuhite, and said, 2 "How long will you set snares for words? Be sensible, and afterward we will speak. 3 Wherefore are we counted as beasts, and reputed vile in your sight? 4 O you who tear yourself in your anger, shall the earth be forsaken for you? or shall the rock be removed out of his place?

18.0.1.en: Then answered Bildad the Shuhite, and said: [1].

18.0.2.en: "How long will you set snares for words?"

18.1.0.en: "Be sensible, and afterward we will speak" [2].

18.1.1.en: Bildad shoots an arrow into Job's heart, accusing him of speaking empty words without sense. In this he includes others with Job, perhaps meaning the two friends Eliphaz and Zophar, or some of those present who perhaps defended Job now and then.

18.1.2.en: Bildad had grown weary of hearing speech, and when his turn came he poured out all that was in his heart of distress, without compassion. Sadly, Bildad often thought that wisdom was the monopoly of his own mind and no one else's, so he was hasty in attacking with words.

18.1.3.en: The Apostle commands us that "every man be swift to hear, slow to speak" (Jas 1:19).

18.1.4.en: After Job, in his prosperity, used to give the final, decisive word like a wise man whose opinions all respected, he now directs to him and those with him that they should speak only after they have become sensible.

18.1.5.en: * Look at those who were busy condemning him. Look at those who want to silence his mouth. This is not the attitude of people seeking consolation for him, but on the contrary those who provoke him and mock him... Do you not see their envy? They count silence a disgrace, and the height of folly.

18.1.6.en: St. John Chrysostom The text in the writings of Pope Gregory (the Great) reads: "Then answered Bildad the Shuhite, and said: To what extent will you utter your words and spread them abroad? First understand, let us speak" [1-2]. In most of his interpretation of the Book of Job, this Father sees Job as a symbol of the holy Church, and his friends as symbols of the heretics who oppose her.

18.1.7.en: Here Bildad, as a representative of the heretics, brings two accusations against the Church: the first, that her views are not original, and the second, that she is without understanding, as she does not grasp their views and thoughts. In every age, since the Church holds to the living faith without laxity, some accuse her of arrogance, pride and rigidity, and since she rejects dissolute views, they accuse her of narrowness of outlook, unable to be contemporary, as she does not understand what is going on around her.

18.1.8.en: In St. Jerome's comment on the words of the Apostle Paul: "fulfilling the desires of the flesh and of the mind" (Eph 2:3), he distinguishes between the sin of the flesh and the sin of thought, saying: [There is a difference between the sin of the flesh and the sin of the mind. The sin of the flesh is immodest and licentious, and acts as an instrument for the fulfillment of its lusts. But the iniquity of the mind concerns teaching against the truth and the decline of the heretics.]

18.1.9.en: * All heretics think that the holy Church, because she knows some things, is full of pride, while they count her as not understanding some things which they imagine. Thus Bildad the Shuhite was like one asserting that the blessed Job had been broken down in pride, when he declared that he "spreads words abroad." But (Bildad himself) bears a sign of his own pride, for he was puffed up, supposing that the blessed Job utters things he does not understand.

18.1.11.en: Whatever accusations are directed against the Church, she does not cease her continual striving until she brings all the believers to the unity of the faith, which the Apostle Paul counts as attaining to perfection: "Till we all come in the unity of the faith, and of the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ: that we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine" (Eph 4:12-14).

18.1.12.en: St. John Chrysostom comments on these words, saying: [We mature when we attain to the unity of the faith, that is, when there are partakers in the one faith, for this is the unity of the faith, when we all become one, when we all know the same covenant.]

18.2.0.en: "Wherefore are we counted as beasts, and reputed vile in your sight?" [3]

18.2.1.en: It is true that Job called his friends deceivers (Job 17:2), and portrayed them as unwise and without mercy, but he never called them animals or beasts as Bildad claims here. Bildad was offended by Job's rebuke, and counted it a grave insult, so he returned insult with a bitterer and harsher insult.

18.2.2.en: * "Why are we silent before you like beasts?" (LXX) Because you have a beastly spirit, you bow your head toward the earth. Surely your thoughts are not sound, and do not suit honest men, but those of whom David said: ["Man, being in honor, does not understand; he is compared to the irrational herd, and is like them"] (see Ps 49:12).

18.2.3.en: As for Bildad, when he realized that he was unable to answer Job, he turned to abuse, and became a threatening figure at the wrong moment. For this reason Job's words, which he addressed to the adversary (the devil) and not to God, Bildad counted as being against God, and so he was not ashamed to wrong the righteous man.

18.2.4.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * Since all heretics complain that the holy Church despises them in her estimate of them, he added: ["So we are counted as beasts, and as corrupt in your eyes"] [3]. It is natural for the human mind to suppose that the things it does come back upon it. So they believe that they are despised, as they are accustomed to despise the ways of the righteous... The Church proves against the heretics that what they do is unreasonable, so they think within themselves that the Church looks upon them as beasts.

18.3.0.en: "O you who tear yourself in your anger, shall the earth be forsaken for you? or shall the rock be removed out of his place?" [4]

18.3.1.en: Bildad became still more enraged and counted Job a fierce animal: "O you who tear yourself in your anger." If Job was a beast of prey, he tore himself. Perhaps Bildad wished to answer Job, who had accused God: "His wrath has devoured me and persecuted me," by saying: [Do not blame God as though He had devoured you; rather by your own savagery you have devoured yourself.]

18.3.2.en: Bildad accused Job of arrogance, as if he could legislate for God: "Shall the earth be forsaken (abandoned) for you?", as if he wished the laws of nature to be changed for him alone. Or as if the world could not stand without him, so that if he perished the world would perish with him, and the earth be emptied with him.

18.3.3.en: Some see that Bildad rebukes Job thus: either he confesses that he is wicked and deserves what has come upon him, or he supposes that God has abandoned His divine providence and forsaken the earth, and that the rock of ages has been removed.

18.3.4.en: In mockery the heretics speak with the Church as Bildad speaks here with Job. It is as though they say to her: [Do you think that you alone are the ark of salvation, and that without you no man will enjoy divine salvation? What you proclaim is a kind of madness and pride.]

18.3.5.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) comments on this text, saying:

18.3.6.en: [The heretics count that the strong feelings of good order or of the spiritual grace of holy preaching are not good as a virtue, but are the madness of anger...

18.3.7.en: "Shall the earth be forsaken for you?" (Job 18:4)... The holy catholic Church declares that God cannot be worshiped except through her, affirming that all who are outside her will not be saved. And the heretics, on the other hand, trusting that they can be saved even without entering her bounds, assert that divine help reaches them everywhere...

18.3.8.en: "Or shall the rock be removed out of his place?" The heretics call these persons rocks, those who in their view, by the loftiness of their thoughts, stand in the human race boasting of being teachers. But the holy Church offers herself to gather together the erring preachers so that they may enter together into the bosom of sound faith. What is this counted as but that she [moves the rock from its place]. And when they gain a sound view of things, they submit humbly within her, those who formerly took a stubborn stance, holding fast to erroneous concepts...?

18.3.9.en: Thus Bildad bore a symbol of the heretics who were exalted on the ground that their life is happy, puffed up over the blows that befell the blessed Job.]

18.3.10.en: Rahab and her household would not have enjoyed salvation had they gone out of the house on whose window the scarlet thread was hung, for there is no salvation outside the Church redeemed by the blood of Christ.

18.3.11.en: * Rahab represents the Church, and the scarlet cord signifies the blood of Christ, and only those in the house were saved. Whoever wishes to be saved, let him come to this house where the blood of Christ is the sign of redemption... Let no one deceive himself, for no one is saved outside the house, I mean outside the Church.

18.3.12.en: Origen * Do you think you can stand and live if you withdraw to set up for yourselves various houses and places, when it was said to Rahab: "Bring thou thy father, and thy mother, and thy brethren, and all thy father's household, home unto thee into the house: and it shall be, that whosoever shall go out of the doors of thy house into the street, his blood shall be upon his head, and we will be guiltless"?!

18.3.13.en: * In this the mystery was declared, that those who wish to live and escape the destruction of the world must gather together in one house alone, that is, in the Church, but whoever goes out from among those gathered there together, that is, if anyone, although he received grace in the Church, leaves it and goes outside, his blood is upon his own head; he is responsible for the destruction of his own soul, which Paul made clear when he commanded us to avoid the heretic (Rom 16:17).

18.3.14.en: * Whoever remains outside the Church is outside the camp of Christ.

18.3.15.en: * He is not a Christian who is not within the Church of Christ.

18.3.16.en: * For how can anyone be with Christ if he does not walk within the Bride of Christ, and is not found in His Church?!

18.3.17.en: * He who does not have the Church as his mother cannot have God as his Father!

18.4.s.en: 2. The light of the wicked is put out

18.4.0.en: 5 "Yea, the light of the wicked shall be put out, and the flame of his fire shall not shine. 6 The light shall be dark in his tabernacle, and his lamp above him is put out.

18.4.1.en: "Yea, the light of the wicked shall be put out, and the flame of his fire shall not shine" [5].

18.4.2.en: Bildad's speech here is true, but it is not fulfilled immediately and in a visible, public manner.

18.4.3.en: By saying "Yea," Bildad refers to what Job suffers of the intense grief under which he has fallen. He says to him: What you say is true, for you ought to be as you are, as a natural thing fitting for a wicked man. So do not be astonished if the little light you had has been completely put out. Perhaps by the light of the wicked he meant the good things and joy he had for a short time before the trials came. The light of the wicked is not the light of the eternal Sun of righteousness, the light of the Lord which will never go out, but is ["the light of his fire, and the spark he kindled"] (Isa 50:11).

18.4.4.en: Job speaks of the days of his prosperity when the lamp of the Lord shone upon his head (Job 29:3). And the psalmist David says: "For thou wilt light my candle: the LORD my God will enlighten my darkness" (Ps 18:28). On the other hand, the righteous Job expresses his intense pain by saying: "How oft is the candle of the wicked put out!" (Job 21:17). And Solomon says: "Whoso curseth his father or his mother, his lamp shall be put out in obscure darkness" (Prov 20:20). "The lamp of the wicked shall be put out" (Prov 24:20). The Lord Christ pointed to deprivation of the Kingdom of God, or the kingdom of light, by entering into outer darkness or hell (Mt 8:12; 22:13).

18.4.5.en: It is said in the Proverbs: "The light of the righteous rejoiceth: but the lamp of the wicked shall be put out" (Prov 13:9; see Jer 25:10).

18.4.6.en: * ["Shall not the light of the wicked be put out, and the flame of his fire not shine?"] [5]. If he says this of the present life, he is mistaken, for often light is seen flourishing in the life of the wicked, while the darkness of shame and poverty envelops the life of the righteous... And if this is said regarding the wicked man, it is not directed against the holy man upon whom blows fall...

18.4.7.en: But "the light of the wicked is put out" in that the happiness of the present life soon ends with life itself. Therefore it is fitting to add: "and the flame of his fire shall not shine." For every wicked man has "the flame of his fire," which he kindles in his heart from the heat of temporal lusts, as long as he burns with various desires, and scatters his thoughts in a greater flame with the manifold illusions of the world. But if the fire is without flame, it does not shine by giving off any light... For even the righteous have the flame of their fire, but it is a flame that lights with brightness, since their desires shine forth in good works. But the light of the wicked does not shine, at least as they would wish in evil, and they are bound to enter into darkness.

18.4.9.en: The enemy of good, the devil, cannot give light, and if he appears to give light, he bears a counterfeit light. For he is the ruler of the kingdom of darkness, and appears as an angel of light to deceive mankind and bring it into the kingdom of darkness. So the wicked, who persist in their disobedience, will not be able to give light, for they offer of what is theirs and their father's, that is, darkness.

18.4.10.en: * Since we know Christ to be the true Light (Jn 1:9), He is not comprehended (1 Tim 6:16) by falsehood. We learn this, that it is necessary for our life also to be enlightened by the rays of the true Light. But the virtues are the rays of the "Sun of righteousness" (Mal 4:2), sent forth for our enlightenment, through which we put off the works of darkness (2 Cor 4:2). When we do everything in the light, we ourselves become light, shining upon others (Mt 5:15-16), for this is the characteristic of light.

18.4.11.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa * Satan does not aim his arrows in the daytime lest he be seen, for everything done in the light is made manifest by the light.

18.4.12.en: * The heretics do not have Christ, the Truth, on their lips, because He is not in their hearts... They mean one thing in their hearts, and promise another on their tongues. They speak of godliness, and hide evil. They speak of Christ, and conceal the antichrist, for they know that they will not succeed in deceiving if they show the antichrist. They offer light only to hide the darkness, for by the light they lead into darkness.

18.5.0.en: St. Jerome "The light shall be dark in his tabernacle, and his lamp above him is put out" [6].

18.5.1.en: He means here the tabernacle of the soul (2 Cor 5:1), that is, the body, which is wholly corrupted and becomes darkness.

18.5.2.en: If the tabernacle is the body, then the removal of the lamp refers to death, for "when a wicked man dieth, his expectation shall perish" (Prov 11:7).

18.5.3.en: The wicked think that life is the enjoyment of fleshly lusts, pleasures and amusement, and that deprivation of them is loss of life, or they see them as their light, without which they would be like dwellers in gloomy graves. What they count as light grows dark, and what they think a lamp is put out.

18.5.4.en: This is the light of the wicked and their lamp, but the light of true believers is the word of God, which dispels the darkness, and makes the believers a true light in the Lord.

18.5.5.en: * The lamp is a light in an earthen vessel, but the light in the earthen vessel is the pleasure in the body. So the lamp that is above him is put out, since the recompense for his evil comes upon the wicked man, and bodily pleasure becomes nothing in the heart.

18.6.0.en: "The steps of his strength shall be straitened, and his own counsel shall cast him down" [7].

18.6.1.en: Since the wicked man devotes all his energies to temporal goods, heedless of eternal blessings, his days pass like a shadow, and the steps of his life are counted very short, and he goes out empty-handed. And since he spends all his effort thinking about temporal things, his plans turn into an enemy to him, depriving him of true, eternal life.

18.6.2.en: * "And his own counsel shall cast him down" [7]. Every wicked man's counsel aims at temporal things, leaving eternal things aside, so he practices injustice and mocks righteousness. But when the Judge of the righteous and the unjust comes, every wicked person is cast down by his own counsel, for his choice of the things to come was with evil intent, therefore he is cast down, sunk in the darkness of eternal woe.

18.6.4.en: * The love of this world is a harlot, who seduces by the desire of her beauty those who hold her to love her. The man whom the love of the world possesses and who falls into her snares cannot save his soul from her embrace until his soul is plundered. When the world strips man of everything, and throws him out of his dwelling on the day of his death, only then does man understand that he has truly been deceived and led astray.

18.6.5.en: * As long as man approaches this world on the path of his life, love of material things strikes its roots in him. He is always troubled and anxious over them, and for their sake he fights others, and the friendship of certain persons captivates him... Let us remember this, beloved, and let us make light of the things that are here as far as possible, and so withdraw our thoughts gradually toward the things to come. If we do not control ourselves little by little, we shall have no strength to renounce bodily things so as to look to God St. Isaac the Syrian * If the fashion of the world passes away (1 Cor 7:31), then without doubt everything in the world will come to an end. All will pass. Every day the world grows older Fr. Ambrosiaster

18.7.0.en: 8 For his feet push him into the net, and he walks into a mesh. 9 The snare grasps him by the heel, and the nets hold him fast. 10 The snare is laid for him in the ground, and a trap for him in the way.

18.7.1.en: "For his feet push him into the net (into the snare), and he walks into a mesh" [8].

18.7.2.en: The wicked man's strong plans and mighty efforts fail, for his sinful ways drive him into evil, so he does not accomplish his purposes. The more effort he puts into his counsel, the more he is entangled in the nets, and hastens to his destruction.

18.7.3.en: * ["For he puts his foot in the net, and walks in its threads"] [8]. He who puts his feet in a net cannot take them out when he thinks to (except by asking God's grace). He who allows himself to sink into the habits of sin cannot rise from them when he wishes. And he who walks in the threads of the net hinders his steps in walking. And when he tries to free himself in order to walk, he finds himself bound and tied, and is unable to walk. It often happens that a man is distracted by the pleasures of this world in order to reach the glories of its honor... but he learns, by obtaining them, how trivial what he sought is. If he returns to himself he sees how he fell into the nets of sin. The very power that entangles him holds him, and he cannot escape from sins... Then he sees in the true light what hard bonds he is bound with. For we do not know even that we are bound, with a sound understanding, until we struggle to be freed, and try to lift our feet...

18.7.5.en: And as many Fathers of the Church affirm, such as St. Macarius the Great, that sin carries its corruption within it, the wicked man who is set on his wickedness perishes as a natural fruit of evil, certain of corruption.

18.7.6.en: The wicked man does not need someone to restrain and punish him, rather what he does gives him bitterness and death! He drinks from the very cup that he has filled for himself, unless he throws away the cup during his enjoyment of fellowship with his Savior, and his earnest striving through the holy will in the Lord.

18.7.7.en: * If you remain in what concerns the dust, you will in the end be turned into it. It is fitting for you to change, you must be transformed, you must become heavenly.

18.7.8.en: Origen * We have all become one lump of clay, a lump of sin. And since we lost our reward through sin, in the absence of God's mercies we deserve, as sinners, nothing but eternal destruction. What man, then, from this lump thinks he is able to ask God, saying: "Why hast thou made me thus?" If you wish to know those things, do not be clay, but be a son of God through the mercy of Him who gives to those who believe in His name the power to become sons of God.

18.7.9.en: * Truly by sin we slide into death. For where the Law forbids, sin is graver than if the Law had not forbidden it. At any rate, where grace is added we can fulfill without difficulty and with our whole will what the Law strictly commands. We are no longer slaves of the Law through fear, but friends and servants of righteousness through love.

18.7.10.en: St. Augustine He who eats and drinks sin falls into snares, and his will is loosened and weakened, and he finds himself a slave to it in humiliation, unable to be saved from it, but thirsting for it. We should not wonder at this, for he who uses drugs, the more he uses them becomes the more a captive in their snares, and his attachment to them increases all the more.

18.7.11.en: Many think that the practice of sin gives them a bitter experience, so they flee from it through their own bitter experience. This reasoning is not sound, for he who tastes sin while perceiving its destruction desires it all the more at the expense of his inner joy and his peace and eternal glory. Sin, like fire, inflames man and shatters his will, so that he cannot be free from it unless God's surpassing grace supports him.

18.8.0.en: "The snare grasps him by the heel, and the nets hold him fast" [9].

18.8.1.en: The wicked man who is set on his evil and on not returning to God cannot escape drinking the bitter cup of evil and reaping its deadly fruit. This is what the Holy Bible sometimes calls divine wrath, or the fulfillment of divine justice. This is the translation of the cherishing of freedom of will, for when man chooses evil by his will, he only keeps for himself the fruit of evil. "The Lord knoweth how ... to reserve the unjust unto the day of judgment to be punished" (2 Pet 2:9).

18.8.2.en: The text in the Septuagint translation reads: ["And the snares hold him, and those who thirst strengthen themselves toward his destruction"] [9 LXX].

18.8.3.en: * ["And the thirsty burn strongly against him"] [9]. When our ancient enemy catches someone alive in the snares of sin, he thirsts for his death. This statement can also be understood in another sense. When the wicked mind sees that it has fallen into sin, it seeks with superficial thought to escape from the snares of sin. But fearing the threats or rebukes of men, it chooses to die eternally rather than suffer slight trials for a while. So the mind surrenders itself entirely to the ways of evil when it sees itself already bound... and the sinner despairs of his return. By this very despair he burns more fiercely in the lusts of this world, the heat of desire rises within him, and the mind fallen in the nets of former sins is inflamed toward a more bitter disobedience. Therefore it was added: ["And the thirsty burn strongly against him"]...

18.8.4.en: The one afflicted with dropsy, the more he drinks, the more his thirst increases, and every covetous person doubles his thirst the more he drinks (of money).

18.9.0.en: "The snare is laid for him in the ground (a cord is hidden for him in the ground), and a trap for him in the way" [10].

18.9.1.en: The misleading enemy of good does not cease to fight mankind by every means of deception, hiding his cords and snares in the paths men walk. His war is hidden and full of deceit, he does not despair of resisting servants and people, old men, children and youths, women and men, virgins and married, rich and poor, sick and healthy. To each one he offers a war that suits him. But as we look to the heavenly One who gives victory, we do not fear the tricks and deceptions of the devil.

18.9.2.en: * "Their snares are hidden in the ground, and all their cords are in the way" [10 LXX]. This is true, for Satan hides the nets in the earth in such a way that he uses those who are deceived, that is, those who live according to the wisdom of the world (1 Cor 2:6; 3:9), and according to the lusts of men (1 Pet 4:2; 2 Pet 1:4). He (Satan) sets the accuser, those around him, on the way, that is, by all the ways of men. For he wants to catch them and take them captive by every means. He catches the righteous man by self-righteousness, and the sinner by his greed. David sings prophetically: ["They spread their cords as a net for my feet, they set a stumbling block for me beside the way"] (Ps 140:5). Even Bildad, who uttered what was upright in his earlier statements, came to lie in the following words.

18.9.3.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * His snare is hidden in the ground when sin is concealed under earthly concerns, because our enemy, in carrying out his plans, shows the human mind a longing for earthly gain, and hides the snare of sin until it binds itself completely... The enemy of mankind surveys the inclinations of each individual to see with which evils he is allied, and the enemy places these things before his face, where he sees the mind drawn to them. To those of a gentle and cheerful temperament he often suggests dissoluteness, and sometimes vainglory, but to those of a violent temperament he suggests pride or violence. He sets the snare where he sees the way the mind is heading.

18.9.5.en: * We have warned you beforehand to take care lest the evil spirits deceive you and turn you away from reading and understanding what we say. For they strive to hold you as slaves and servants. At times they use appearances in dreams and magical deceptions to subdue all those who fail to exert strong opposing efforts for the salvation of their souls.

18.9.6.en: God the Word urges us and strengthens us to keep away from the demons, and to follow the living God alone through His Son.

18.9.7.en: We who for a time wallowed in fornication, now accept chastity alone.

18.9.8.en: We formerly used the arts of magic, and now we dedicate ourselves to the good, living God.

18.9.9.en: Our concern above all was to gain wealth and possessions, and now we bring what we own to be common property for every needy person to take from it.

18.9.10.en: We hated and destroyed one another because of the difference in our manners, for we refused to live with those of another tribe, but today, since the coming of Christ, we live together in familiarity.

18.9.11.en: Today we pray for our enemies, and try to urge those who hate us without cause to submit to the good principles of Christ and His commandments, in order that they may share with us the same joyful hope of receiving a reward offered by God, the Ruler of all.

18.9.12.en: St. Justin the Martyr * Satan is always diligent, even when danger comes upon him of losing his prey.

18.9.13.en: * Satan can destroy even under the appearance of godliness. For he can destroy not only by leading to fornication, but also on the contrary, by the excessive grief that accompanies repentance for fornication. This is his fitting work, to possess us by sin, but to catch us in the net in our repentance is a shame accomplished with great malice, for repentance is our weapon, not his.

18.9.14.en: St. John Chrysostom * The problem is not in recognizing the devil's schemes, but in making a mockery of them. Paul knows the schemes of the demons, not to be occupied with them, but so as not to fall into their snares.

18.9.15.en: St. Didymus the Blind * "And no marvel; for Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light" (2 Cor 11:14)... These deceptions are appearances of that spirit who seeks to cast wretched souls into the nets... and turns them away from the true worship of the true God, who alone can cleanse and heal.

18.9.16.en: * At times Satan changes himself into an angel of light, to test those who need testing, or to deceive those who deserve to be deceived. Only God's great mercies are able to rescue man from the mistaken understanding of evil spirits, so that he thinks them good angels, and of false friends as though they were true, and rescue him from the troubles of all the losses that come because of the utterly deadly satanic deceptions, which cannot be expressed.
